title: After the kettle
hook: habits hook onto cues, so attach practice to something you already do

segments.voice: Yesterday: how long a habit takes. Your line was 66 days, roughly, and one missed day doesn't reset it. Did your practice happen after the moment you chose? Day three hundred eleven.

Think about this morning. You probably didn't decide to reach for your phone when you woke up. Your hand just went there. You didn't decide to put the kettle on or start the coffee. You walked into the kitchen and it happened, the way your foot finds the brake. Nobody used willpower for any of that. The moment did the deciding. That sounds like bad news for anyone trying to build a new practice. It's actually the best news in the whole science of habits. If a moment can pull the old habits out of you, it can pull a new one out too. Today: after the kettle.
screen: `YOUR HAND FINDS THE PHONE.` → `THE MOMENT DOES THE DECIDING.` → `IT CAN PULL A NEW ONE OUT TOO.`

segments.voice: First, how much of the day runs on autopilot. The psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked people to write down what they were doing and thinking through the day. Roughly four in ten actions were done in the same place, almost every day, often while thinking about something else. Habits aren't laziness. They're how a busy brain saves effort. Second, habits hook onto cues. A cue is a place, a time, an object, or the thing you just finished. The kettle clicks, and something follows. So instead of adding a practice to your day as a brand new event, you hang it on a hook that's already there. Third, say it as a plan. The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer studied what he called implementation intentions, plans in the form: if this happens, then I'll do that. Across many studies, people who made a specific if-then plan followed through more often than people who only set a goal. I want to meditate more is a wish. After I switch the kettle on, I sit for two minutes while it boils: that's a plan. Fourth, notice the traditions knew this. So many of the world's practices are tied to cues. The Muslim prayers are set by the sun. Jewish blessings come before bread and after. In many Catholic towns, a church bell rang for the Angelus in the morning, at noon and in the evening. Monks keep hours. Nobody had to remember to be devout at random; the day itself tapped them on the shoulder. So pick your kettle. The cue does the remembering, and you do the practice.
screen: `FOUR IN TEN ACTIONS ON AUTOPILOT.` · `HABITS HOOK ONTO CUES.` · `IF THIS, THEN THAT.` · `THE DAY TAPS THE SHOULDER.` · then, large: `AFTER THE KETTLE.`

segments.voice: Pick your cue now. Walk through tomorrow morning in your mind, slowly, from waking up. Where are the moments that happen every single day? Feet on the floor. The kettle. Unlocking the car. Pick one, the more boring the better. Then finish the sentence: after this, I will do that, for two minutes. Say it once, quietly. Then sit, and let the plan settle. The bell holds the time.
After the kettle. Hang a new practice on something you already do every day, and let the cue do the remembering. Today's word.
Your line: after the kettle. Tomorrow morning, when your cue comes, do the practice right then, even for thirty seconds. Write the sentence somewhere you'll see it tonight. Day three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Many people tie a daily practice to an existing cue, such as sitting for two minutes after switching on the kettle; many traditions set prayer by the sun, the meal or a bell.

fork.setup: you want to sit for two minutes every day. which plan is most likely to stick?
options: after I switch on the kettle, I sit while it boils.
every day, no matter what, somehow.
fork.reveal: a specific cue with a specific action is an implementation intention, and studies find those get followed through more often.

trapdoor: what you thought: build a habit with willpower.
what it means: hang it on a cue you already have, and let the cue remember.
what a scholar hears: Gollwitzer's implementation intentions, if-then plans that a 2006 review found had a medium-to-large effect on follow-through.

Tradition examples are descriptive: Islamic prayer times by the sun, Jewish blessings before and after eating, the Angelus traditionally rung morning, noon and evening, monastic hours. A reviewer from each tradition may want to confirm the wording.
